item.text:
Canada is the world’s second-largest country by area, stretching from the Atlantic Ocean to the Pacific and northward to the Arctic Ocean. It is a geographically immense, culturally diverse, and politically influential country known for its vast wilderness, stable democracy, multicultural society, and close relationship with the United States.

## Geography

Canada covers approximately 9.98 million square kilometres, making it the largest country in the Western Hemisphere and second only to Russia in total area. Despite its size, much of its territory is sparsely populated because of its northern climate and rugged terrain.

The country has ten provinces and three territories:

- Newfoundland and Labrador
- Prince Edward Island
- Nova Scotia
- New Brunswick
- Quebec
- Ontario
- Manitoba
- Saskatchewan
- Alberta
- British Columbia
- Yukon
- Northwest Territories
- Nunavut

Canada has the longest coastline in the world, bordering three oceans: the Atlantic, Pacific, and Arctic. It also contains enormous freshwater resources, including part of the Great Lakes, which Canada shares with the United States. These lakes—Superior, Michigan, Huron, Erie, and Ontario—form one of the largest freshwater systems on Earth.

The landscape varies dramatically. The Atlantic provinces feature rocky coasts, fishing villages, forests, and rolling hills. Quebec and Ontario contain dense forests, major river systems, and important urban corridors. The Prairie provinces are characterized by broad agricultural plains and grasslands. Alberta and British Columbia contain the Rocky Mountains, while British Columbia also has temperate rainforests and a rugged Pacific coastline. Northern Canada includes tundra, glaciers, permafrost, and immense areas of boreal forest.

Canada has numerous major rivers, including the Mackenzie, Yukon, Fraser, Saskatchewan, and St. Lawrence. The St. Lawrence River is especially important because it connects the Great Lakes to the Atlantic Ocean and supports major cities, ports, and industries.

## Climate

Canada has several climate zones. Southern regions generally experience four distinct seasons, with warm summers and cold winters. Coastal British Columbia has relatively mild, rainy winters, while the Prairie provinces are known for dry climates and extreme temperature changes. Atlantic Canada receives considerable precipitation and is influenced by ocean storms.

Northern Canada has long, severe winters and short summers. In the Arctic, some areas experience polar night during winter and continuous daylight during part of the summer. Snow, ice, and permafrost strongly influence transportation, construction, wildlife, and Indigenous communities.

Climate change is especially visible in the Canadian Arctic, where temperatures are rising rapidly. Melting sea ice, thawing permafrost, coastal erosion, and changing wildlife patterns affect northern communities and ecosystems.

## History

Before European colonization, Canada was inhabited by numerous Indigenous peoples with distinct languages, political systems, economies, and cultures. These peoples are commonly grouped into First Nations, Inuit, and Métis, although each category contains many separate nations and communities.

Vikings established a settlement at L’Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland around the year 1000, centuries before later European exploration. Beginning in the late fifteenth and early sixteenth centuries, European explorers and fishing crews reached the Atlantic coast.

France established settlements along the St. Lawrence River, including Quebec City, founded by Samuel de Champlain in 1608. French colonization created New France, whose economy depended heavily on fishing, farming, trade, and the fur trade. French settlers developed relationships and alliances with many Indigenous nations, although these relationships were also shaped by conflict, disease, competition, and displacement.

Britain gradually expanded its influence in North America. The Seven Years’ War ended with Britain gaining control of most French territories in what became Canada. The Royal Proclamation of 1763 recognized certain Indigenous rights and established principles governing the Crown’s relationship with Indigenous peoples, though those principles were often violated or narrowly interpreted.

After the American Revolution, many Loyalists moved north into British North America. The War of 1812 further shaped relations between British North America, Indigenous nations, and the United States.

Canada was formed as a self-governing federation on July 1, 1867, through Confederation. The original provinces were Ontario, Quebec, Nova Scotia, and New Brunswick. Manitoba joined in 1870, British Columbia in 1871, Prince Edward Island in 1873, Alberta and Saskatchewan in 1905, Newfoundland in 1949, and the territories developed through several stages. Nunavut was created in 1999.

The building of the Canadian Pacific Railway helped connect the country from east to west, but it also contributed to the displacement of Indigenous peoples and the exploitation of Chinese workers. Chinese immigrants played a major role in railway construction and later faced discriminatory laws, including the Chinese head tax and exclusion policies.

Canada participated in the First and Second World Wars. Its military contribution, industrial production, and diplomatic development strengthened its international identity. The country later became active in peacekeeping, international diplomacy, NATO, the Commonwealth, and the United Nations.

## Indigenous peoples and reconciliation

Indigenous peoples remain central to Canada’s history and present-day identity. First Nations communities are located across the country, Inuit communities are concentrated in Inuit Nunangat—the Inuit homeland—and Métis communities have a particularly strong historical presence in the Prairie provinces and parts of Ontario and the Northwest.

Colonial policies caused extensive harm. The residential school system separated Indigenous children from their families, suppressed Indigenous languages and cultures, and subjected many children to neglect and abuse. The Truth and Reconciliation Commission of Canada documented these abuses and issued Calls to Action concerning education, justice, health, language, culture, and government relations.

Modern Canada continues to face major challenges involving land claims, treaty interpretation, child welfare, access to clean water, housing, healthcare, incarceration, missing and murdered Indigenous women and girls, and the preservation of Indigenous languages. At the same time, Indigenous nations are exercising growing authority through self-government, legal action, cultural revitalization, economic development, and negotiations over natural resources.

## Government and politics

Canada is a constitutional monarchy and a parliamentary democracy. The monarch is the formal head of state, represented in Canada by the governor general. The prime minister is the head of government and normally leads the political party that holds the most seats in the House of Commons.

Parliament has two chambers:

- The House of Commons, whose members are elected
- The Senate, whose members are appointed

Canada has a federal system. The national government handles matters such as defence, foreign policy, immigration, criminal law, currency, and interprovincial trade. Provincial governments control areas such as education, healthcare administration, property law, and many aspects of natural resources. Municipal governments manage services including local transportation, roads, zoning, water, and waste collection.

Canadian politics often involves regional differences. Ontario and Quebec contain much of the population and economic activity, while the Prairie provinces emphasize agriculture, energy, and resource development. British Columbia has strong Pacific and environmental interests. Atlantic provinces have distinctive concerns involving fisheries, population aging, transportation, and regional economic development. Northern territories face unique issues related to remoteness, infrastructure, Indigenous governance, and climate change.

Major national political debates include healthcare, housing affordability, immigration, climate policy, energy development, Indigenous rights, taxation, national unity, and relations with the United States.

## Languages and culture

Canada has two official federal languages: English and French. English is the majority language in most provinces, while French is dominant in Quebec and has significant communities in New Brunswick, Ontario, Manitoba, and other regions. New Brunswick is officially bilingual.

Quebec has a distinct French-speaking society with its own history, literature, music, media, legal traditions, and political institutions. The province has repeatedly debated its relationship with the rest of Canada, including sovereignty referendums in 1980 and 1995.

Canada is officially multicultural. Immigration has transformed the country’s cities, workplaces, schools, cuisine, arts, and politics. Toronto, Vancouver, Montreal, Calgary, Edmonton, Ottawa, and Winnipeg are notably diverse urban centres. Canadian society includes communities with roots in every major region of the world.

Canadian cultural traditions combine Indigenous, French, British, immigrant, and North American influences. Important cultural expressions include literature, filmmaking, visual arts, theatre, popular music, Indigenous art, winter festivals, and regional food traditions.

Canada has produced internationally recognized writers such as Margaret Atwood, Alice Munro, Michael Ondaatje, Yann Martel, Mordecai Richler, and Louise Erdrich’s work is often discussed in relation to North American Indigenous literature, though she is American. Canadian musicians include Leonard Cohen, Joni Mitchell, Neil Young, Céline Dion, Drake, The Weeknd, Shania Twain, Arcade Fire, and Justin Bieber.

## Economy

Canada has a high-income, diversified economy. Important sectors include:

- Energy
- Mining
- Forestry
- Agriculture
- Manufacturing
- Finance
- Technology
- Telecommunications
- Tourism
- Education
- Healthcare
- Professional services

Canada is one of the world’s major producers of oil, natural gas, uranium, potash, nickel, gold, lumber, wheat, canola, seafood, and other commodities. Alberta is especially important for oil and gas, Saskatchewan for potash and agriculture, British Columbia for forestry and mining, and the Atlantic provinces for fisheries and offshore resources.

Ontario has a large manufacturing, finance, technology, and services economy. Toronto is Canada’s largest financial centre. Montreal is important for aerospace, artificial intelligence, pharmaceuticals, design, and culture. Vancouver has strong technology, film, shipping, tourism, forestry, and real-estate sectors.

Canada’s economy is deeply connected to the United States. The two countries share extensive supply chains in automobiles, energy, agriculture, aerospace, technology, and manufacturing. Canada also trades significantly with the European Union, China, Japan, Mexico, South Korea, and other countries.

Economic challenges include dependence on commodity prices, regional inequality, housing costs, limited productivity growth, infrastructure needs, labour shortages, and the difficulty of balancing environmental protection with resource development.

## Healthcare and education

Canada has a publicly funded healthcare system. Provinces and territories administer healthcare, while the federal government provides funding and establishes national principles through the Canada Health Act. Medically necessary hospital and physician services are generally covered for eligible residents, although dental care, prescription drugs, vision care, and mental-health services may have varying levels of coverage.

The system is valued for broad access, but it faces challenges such as long wait times, shortages of family doctors, pressure on emergency departments, uneven rural and northern access, and difficulties recruiting healthcare workers.

Education is primarily a provincial responsibility. Canada has publicly funded primary and secondary education, along with universities, colleges, technical institutes, and apprenticeship systems. Major universities include the University of Toronto, McGill University, the University of British Columbia, the University of Alberta, Université de Montréal, Queen’s University, and the University of Waterloo.

Canada attracts many international students and has a strong reputation in higher education. However, tuition, housing costs, and access to education differ significantly by region.

## Cities

Ottawa is the national capital and the seat of Parliament, the federal government, and many national institutions.

Toronto is the largest city and a major financial, cultural, media, and commercial centre. It is one of the most ethnically diverse cities in the world.

Montreal is the largest city in Quebec and a centre of French-language culture, festivals, design, higher education, aerospace, and technology.

Vancouver is situated between mountains and the Pacific Ocean. It is known for its natural beauty, international population, film industry, technology sector, and high housing costs.

Calgary is a major energy, business, and transportation centre. It also hosts the Calgary Stampede, one of Canada’s best-known annual events.

Edmonton is Alberta’s capital and an important centre for government, education, healthcare, culture, and energy services.

Winnipeg is a central transportation hub with significant Indigenous, Métis, agricultural, and cultural importance.

Halifax is the largest city in Atlantic Canada and a major naval, educational, shipping, and cultural centre.

Quebec City is known for its historic architecture, fortified old city, and importance in French Canadian history.

## Nature and wildlife

Canada contains vast protected areas and diverse ecosystems. Its forests support species such as black bears, grizzly bears, moose, caribou, wolves, lynx, beavers, and numerous bird species. Coastal and Arctic waters contain whales, seals, walruses, polar bears, and seabirds.

The beaver is one of Canada’s best-known symbols and played a major historical role in the fur trade. The maple leaf is the country’s national symbol and appears on the Canadian flag.

Canada has many famous national parks, including Banff and Jasper in Alberta, Yoho and Pacific Rim in British Columbia, Gros Morne in Newfoundland and Labrador, Fundy in New Brunswick, and Wood Buffalo in Alberta and the Northwest Territories. These parks protect mountains, glaciers, forests, grasslands, wetlands, fjords, and Arctic environments.

Wildlife conservation is complicated by habitat loss, climate change, industrial development, pollution, invasive species, and conflicts between animals and human communities. Conservation efforts include protected areas, Indigenous stewardship, species recovery programs, and international cooperation.

## Sports

Ice hockey is deeply associated with Canadian identity, although it is only one part of the country’s sporting culture. Canada has produced many famous hockey players and has a strong professional, amateur, university, and youth hockey system.

Other popular sports include lacrosse, basketball, baseball, soccer, curling, skiing, snowboarding, figure skating, speed skating, football, and Canadian football. Lacrosse is recognized as Canada’s national summer sport, while ice hockey is the national winter sport.

Canada has hosted the Olympic Games in Montreal in 1976, Calgary in 1988, and Vancouver in 2010. It has also hosted major international events such as the FIFA Women’s World Cup, the Pan American Games, and the 2026 FIFA World Cup alongside the United States and Mexico.

## National identity

Canadian identity is difficult to reduce to a single idea because the country contains many regional, linguistic, ethnic, Indigenous, and cultural identities. Commonly associated values include social pluralism, public institutions, political compromise, bilingualism, multiculturalism, and attachment to nature.

Canada is often perceived internationally as peaceful and cooperative, but its history also includes colonialism, discrimination, forced assimilation, exclusionary immigration policies, and unequal treatment of minorities. A complete understanding of Canada requires recognizing both its democratic achievements and its unresolved injustices.

At its best, Canada represents an ongoing attempt to build a large, diverse federation in which different languages, cultures, nations, and regions can coexist. Its future will depend heavily on reconciliation with Indigenous peoples, adaptation to climate change, housing and economic reform, the changing relationship with the United States, and the successful integration of new generations of immigrants.
